NEW YORK (CNN) -- Olympic gold medalist Michael Phelps has acknowledged he engaged in "regrettable" behavior and "demonstrated bad judgment," after a British newspaper published a photograph of the swimmer smoking from a bong. Sports attorney Ryan Smith thinks Michael Phelps should speak to public about his opposition to drug use. Ryan Smith, a sports attorney and BET talk show host, on Monday spoke to John Roberts on CNN's "American Morning" about how the incident could affect Phelps' career. John Roberts: What was your reaction to news of this picture of Michael Phelps surfacing? Ryan Smith: The thing with Michael Phelps is, he's not only been an outspoken athlete against drugs so he's done a lot of testing, he's been supportive of WADA, which is the World Anti-Doping Agency. But he's really a guy of high character. So you look at this, and my first thought was, "What about his endorsement deals? What's going to happen in those?" A lot of endorsement deals have clauses that say that you can't do bad actions like this, not only crimes, but just things that you do bad in public could result in the termination of your contract. So he could lose a lot of money on this. Roberts: Now he never really admitted to smoking marijuana. ... The United States Olympic Committee isn't going to sanction him, it looks like, but did call his actions disappointing. But to the greater issue that you were talking about, in terms of his endorsement deals, do you think anybody is going to say, well, this is the straw that broke the camel's back with this guy? He had one incident back in 2004. But are you going to dump Michael Phelps because of this picture? Smith: It could happen, and the reason why is because a lot of these companies that are sponsoring him really are focused on kids and how actions of their athletes affect children. So that can be a big problem. The other thing is, unlike an athlete that plays sports every year in the public spotlight, the Olympics for swimmers comes only every four years. So he doesn't have that chance to rehabilitate his image immediately like a lot of other athletes, a basketball player or a football player would. So companies might say, you know what, let's not work with Michael Phelps right now, because he doesn't really have a chance to redeem himself. A picture says a thousand words, and how can he fight that? Roberts: How could you turn this around? If you were his attorney, if you were advising him what would you do? Smith: The first thing I would suggest is a drug test. And I know that that's not required. And I also know that he's not really going to have a problem with swimming in 2012. But I would just show that hey, I'm clean, I'm doing great. The next thing I would do is go out there in the public and talk about the troubles with working with drugs and really show the public that you are not about drug use, you are not about doing bad things in public. You are only about supporting the rules of WADA, the World Anti-Doping Agency, and supporting their drug testing program. So you can show that, hey, this is a minor incident, not a big deal. And really what it's all about is remaining clean. Roberts: If you were to lay a bet, would you say anybody drops him? Smith: I would say he'll have some problems. I don't know if I would say that a big sponsor would drop him, but I would say that a more wholesome-oriented sponsor might.

**NEW YORK (CNN) —** Olympic gold medalist Michael Phelps has acknowledged engaging in “regrettable” behavior and demonstrating “bad judgment” after a British newspaper published a photograph of the swimmer smoking from a bong.

Sports attorney Ryan Smith believes Phelps should speak publicly about his opposition to drug use. On Monday, Smith, a sports attorney and BET talk-show host, spoke with John Roberts on CNN’s *American Morning* about how the incident could affect Phelps’ career.

**John Roberts:** What was your reaction when you learned that this picture of Michael Phelps had surfaced?

**Ryan Smith:** The thing about Michael Phelps is that he has not only been an outspoken athlete against drugs—he has also undergone extensive testing and supported WADA, the World Anti-Doping Agency. He is also widely regarded as a person of high character.

When I saw this, my first thought was: “What about his endorsement deals? What is going to happen to them?” Many endorsement agreements contain clauses prohibiting this kind of behavior—not only criminal activity, but also public conduct that reflects poorly on the sponsor. Such actions could result in the termination of a contract, so he could lose a great deal of money over this.

**Roberts:** He never actually admitted to smoking marijuana. The United States Olympic Committee does not appear likely to sanction him, although it did call his actions disappointing. But regarding the broader issue you mentioned—his endorsement deals—do you think anyone will say this is the straw that broke the camel’s back? He had one incident in 2004, but would a company really drop Michael Phelps because of this picture?

**Smith:** It could happen. Many of the companies sponsoring him are focused on children and on how athletes’ actions affect young people, so this could be a significant problem.

Another issue is that, unlike athletes who compete every year in the public spotlight, Olympic swimmers have that level of exposure only once every four years. As a result, he does not have the same opportunity to rehabilitate his image immediately that a basketball or football player might have.

Companies may say, “You know what? Let’s not work with Michael Phelps right now,” because he does not really have an immediate opportunity to redeem himself. A picture is worth a thousand words—how can he fight that?

**Roberts:** How could he turn this around? If you were his attorney and were advising him, what would you recommend?

**Smith:** The first thing I would suggest is a drug test. I know it is not required, and I also know that he is not likely to have a problem competing in swimming in 2012. Still, I would want him to demonstrate: “I’m clean, and I’m doing well.”

Next, I would advise him to speak publicly about the problems associated with drugs and to show that he does not support drug use or inappropriate public behavior. He should emphasize that he supports the rules of WADA, the World Anti-Doping Agency, as well as its drug-testing program.

That would allow him to show that this was a minor incident rather than a major issue. Ultimately, what matters is remaining clean.

**Roberts:** If you had to place a bet, would you say any sponsor will drop him?

**Smith:** I would say he will face some problems. I do not know whether a major sponsor will drop him, but a sponsor with a more wholesome image might.

**NEW YORK (CNN) —** After a British newspaper printed an image that appeared to show Olympic swimming champion Michael Phelps using a bong, Phelps conceded that he had acted in a way he regretted and had shown poor judgment.

Sports lawyer and BET talk-show presenter Ryan Smith said Phelps should publicly emphasize that he does not support drug use. On Monday, Smith joined John Roberts on CNN’s *American Morning* to discuss the possible consequences for Phelps’ career.

**John Roberts:** What did you think when you first heard that this photograph of Michael Phelps had emerged?

**Ryan Smith:** Phelps has publicly opposed drugs, undergone extensive testing and supported the World Anti-Doping Agency, or WADA. He has also been viewed as someone with strong character. Because of that, my immediate concern was what the image could mean for his sponsorship agreements. Many endorsement contracts include morality provisions allowing companies to end a deal not only over criminal conduct, but also over publicly inappropriate behavior. As a result, Phelps could potentially lose a substantial amount of money.

**Roberts:** Phelps did not explicitly say that he had smoked marijuana. It also appears that the United States Olympic Committee will not discipline him, although it described his conduct as disappointing. Turning to the sponsorship issue, do you think any company might decide this is the final incident it is willing to tolerate? There was also an episode in 2004, but would a sponsor really cut ties with Michael Phelps over this photograph?

**Smith:** That is possible. Many of the businesses backing him place a strong emphasis on children and on the influence athletes’ behavior can have on young people, which could make this especially troublesome. Another difficulty is that swimmers do not remain in the public eye through annual seasons in the way that basketball or football players do. The Olympics occur only once every four years, so Phelps cannot quickly repair his reputation through competition as athletes in other sports might. Some companies could therefore decide to stop working with him for now because he has no immediate opportunity to restore his image. The photograph itself is powerful evidence, and it is difficult to counter what people believe they see.

**Roberts:** What could he do to improve the situation? If you represented him, what advice would you give?

**Smith:** I would first recommend that he take a drug test, even though he is not obligated to do so and the incident is unlikely to prevent him from competing in swimming in 2012. A negative result would allow him to demonstrate that he is drug-free and doing well. I would then advise him to address the public, discuss the problems associated with drugs and make clear that he neither supports drug use nor approves of inappropriate public behavior. He should reaffirm his commitment to WADA’s rules and drug-testing system. That approach could help portray this as an isolated, relatively minor event and reinforce that the key issue is staying clean.

**Roberts:** If you had to predict the outcome, do you think any sponsors will drop him?

**Smith:** I expect him to encounter some difficulties. I am not sure that one of his major sponsors will end its relationship with him, but a company with a particularly family-friendly or wholesome image might do so.

## Phelps apologizes for ‘regrettable’ behavior as sponsors weigh response

**BALTIMORE —** Olympic swimming champion Michael Phelps has apologized for what he called “regrettable” behavior after a photograph appeared to show him using a marijuana pipe at a college party.

“I engaged in behavior which was regrettable and demonstrated bad judgment,” Phelps said in a statement. The record-setting swimmer added that he was 23 years old and had acted in a “youthful and inappropriate” way.

The incident created an immediate challenge for Phelps, whose eight gold medals at the 2008 Beijing Olympics turned him into one of the world’s most marketable athletes.

In an interview about the possible fallout, sports-marketing experts said sponsors would have to decide whether the episode represented a temporary lapse or a broader risk to their brands. Their response, experts said, would depend in part on how quickly and convincingly Phelps accepted responsibility.

Several companies initially expressed support for the swimmer. Speedo said Phelps remained a valued member of its team, while luxury watchmaker Omega described the incident as a private matter. Visa also continued its relationship with him. Kellogg, however, said it would not renew its endorsement agreement, saying Phelps’ conduct was inconsistent with the image it wanted to promote.

USA Swimming suspended Phelps from competition for three months, saying the action was intended to send a strong message rather than to punish him for a specific anti-doping violation.

Image-rehabilitation specialists said Phelps’ apology was an important first step but would not, by itself, erase the damage. They said he would need to avoid excuses, demonstrate better judgment and allow his future conduct—in training, competition and public appearances—to support his words.

For sponsors, the calculation extends beyond the photograph itself. Phelps’ appeal was built not only on athletic dominance but also on a disciplined, family-friendly image. The controversy forced companies to assess whether consumers would view the behavior as an isolated mistake or as a betrayal of that image.

Phelps’ competitive legacy remains extraordinary. He won eight gold medals in Beijing, surpassing Mark Spitz’s record of seven at a single Olympic Games. But the episode showed how quickly an athlete’s reputation away from competition can affect a commercial brand built over years.

The swimmer said he was sorry for letting down his family, teammates and supporters. Whether the apology restores public confidence will depend largely on what comes next, marketing experts said: sustained accountability, a clean record and a return to the pool without further controversy.
